text: The crossbow was aimed at a judge, and the man holding it taught mathematics. Kim Kyung-ho had been dismissed from his university, had appealed, and had lost; Chung Ji-young works from the public record of what happened next, and gives himself a hundred minutes, which for a legal fight this documented is close quarters. Filing the story as crime as well as drama is a decision, and it starts the audience's sympathies moving before the first hearing. A film built from this material lives in corridors and hearing rooms, where the only available action is the question of who may speak, and for how long. A man who has spent a career on proofs will not concede a step he considers unearned. Court calendars are not built for that kind of patience, and neither are the people who keep them.

Dave, Noddy, Jim and Don have a band called Flame and one route out of the north of England. Richard Loncraine spends most of ninety-one minutes away from the stage, on the transactions around it: who signs, who is owed, who decides where the group plays next. The film was made in 1975 about the seventies, which is no distance at all — the clubs and the industry it describes were still running while it shot. Rise and fall are both announced in advance, which frees it from suspense and leaves it curious about mechanics instead. Nobody in it is above the offer on the table. They take it, argue about the terms afterwards, take the next one, and the arithmetic underneath — a wage, a week booked or not booked — stays audible under the volume.

Sandy Wilcox is not yet a teenager, lives in rural British Columbia in the 1950s, and shares a first name with the film's director. She wants to be treated as an adult about a year before anyone around her is prepared to try. Then Butch Walker arrives from the United States, older, a cousin, and American, which in that house is qualification enough to reorganise a summer. Ninety minutes, scaled to what a family remembers rather than what a town reports. The Academy of Canadian Cinema and Television gave it best motion picture, an odd prize for a film whose largest event is a visit, and the oddity is the recommendation. Sandy Wilson is exact about one thing: what it is to be watched by someone whose opinion has suddenly outranked a parent's. Not first love. The discovery that a life can be looked at from outside and found small.

A man walks out of his own wedding because he hears someone calling for help. Abdollah had waited years for the marriage, and Shahram Asadi puts the interruption inside the ceremony itself, so that everything afterwards is measured against a room where the guests are still standing and the day is not finished. The genre line reads adventure, drama and fantasy at once, and in Iran in 1994 that is not hedging: it means the road is allowed to bend, and that the truth Abdollah goes out to find may not be the kind admissible anywhere. A hundred and five minutes for a single day. It took the Crystal Simorgh for best film. The pressure worth watching is not on the traveller, who at least has a direction, but on the household he left in the middle of a sentence.

Suellen works a toll booth on the road to the coast, and she has decided what her son needs. He needs an expensive workshop that promises to make him straight, so she starts telling a crew of thieves which cars are worth stopping and which wrists are worth the risk. Carolina Markowicz lays the arrangement out at room temperature. The stealing is small, repetitive, nearly clerical — done from a booth, in a uniform, beside a barrier that lifts. The money is love, aimed with total conviction in the worst direction available. Pedágio runs a hundred and two minutes and took best film at the Grande Prêmio do Cinema Brasileiro. A toll booth is a good place to put a camera: everyone passing through is briefly on the way somewhere better, and everyone stops to pay.

Early in the twentieth century, a Swedish farmer's daughter decided she was going to fly. Elsa Andersson existed; the film Jan Troell built around her is largely invented, and it takes a hundred and fifty-four minutes over a life she is trying to get out of. That ratio is the method. Flight, in that decade, was not a montage: it was money, permission, a father's opinion, a village's opinion, and years of ordinary labour continuing on schedule while a person waits. Troell gives the waiting as much room as the wanting, so the ambition arrives worn down before it is ever tested. Så vit som en snö took the Guldbagge for best film. What holds the length together is not the aviation but the ground it gets measured against: the barn, the season, a household that has always assumed she will stay.

General Kwak had already left the army when the Japanese landed, so he raised a small one of his own. Lee Doo-yong filed his 1973 picture as history and seems to mean it: early Chosun, a province under invasion, a commander with no commission, no treasury, and no authority beyond what the men in front of him grant. That is a different problem from the one a standing army solves. Every recruit is a decision, and a decision can be reversed by morning. Raising troops is a civil act before it is a military one — letters, favours, standing in a yard and asking. The Grand Bell named it best film. What stays interesting is the week before the battle, when a retired man with a reputation has to convert it into something that will hold a line.

Three children smuggle a runaway bride into the house, and the house was already struggling. Rahul took his late sister's children in and is plainly outmatched by them; they are not decoration here, they are the ones who manufacture the crisis, and the crisis is a stranger nobody can account for. Mahesh Bhatt runs a hundred and sixty-three minutes across family, comedy, romance and drama at once, which in 1993 Hindi cinema is not indecision but an agreement about how long an evening lasts and how much feeling it holds. Filmfare gave it best film. What holds attention is the household ledger: a man with no training for any of this, three dependents who outnumber and outmanoeuvre him, and a woman under his roof whose reasons for running have not gone anywhere.

Somebody has to own the murder, and Balwant Rai arranges for it to be Ajay. Prison follows, then the three men Ajay meets inside, then the part the audience has been waiting for. Rajkumar Santoshi's 1990 film takes two hours and forty-three minutes, and the structure is the interest: before a revenge picture can move, every legitimate door has to be shut, and this one shuts them on the record, in daylight, with a name attached to the shutting. The friendships made in prison are the only currency a convicted man has left. Filmfare gave it best film, a mainstream top prize going to a story that opens with the law getting it comprehensively wrong. The wrong is documented; the correction cannot be. That gap is what the remaining hours are for.

An elderly shop porter comes into a little money and spends it on hiring a butler. Harry has no house worth staffing and no dinners worth serving; what he wants is to be looked after properly for a while, by a man who knows how it is done. The inheritance reaches him from a relative he never knew, after several sets of professional hands take their percentage on the way, and that detail says as much about 1961 as the comedy does. Bent Christensen sets a servant of the upper class down among Harry's drinking companions and the neighbourhood's difficult children, and lets him be good at his job. Denmark sent it to the Academy Awards. A hundred and one minutes, filed as family comedy, and kinder than the class premise threatens: the joke is never that Harry does not belong.

Steffen has finished school, has not found work, and is not easily knocked off course. He lives with his mother, a newspaper reporter, widowed; his girlfriend resents the time he gives to Charly, who has come out of a reform school. Denmark, 1978, ninety-eight minutes, shaped week to week rather than plotted. Henning Kristiansen is after temperament instead of incident: how someone of unusual evenness absorbs what the people around him bring him, including a mother's grief arriving at the wrong hour of the night and wearing his father's face. The film was Denmark's submission to the Academy Awards. Its subject is not delinquency, though a reform-school boy is in it, and not first love, though a girlfriend is. It is what steadiness costs the person supplying it.

Twelve orphans live in a mortgaged house, kept there by a man who was abandoned as a child himself. Brahmachari did not inherit that household; he assembled it, and the mortgage is the fact the film will not let him forget. Then he stops a woman from dying, and it emerges that she has business of her own to settle first. Bhappi Sonie takes a hundred and fifty-seven minutes over it, comedy and drama sharing the same rooms rather than alternating. Filmfare gave it best film. The children are not there to be touching. They are the reason a man with nothing cannot walk away from a debt, and the woman is not relief but weight: she brings her past into a house with no spare capacity for it.

The apartment belongs to Julie, the match tickets are out of reach, and nobody goes home. Steffen, Thomas and Mogens have organised a week around football and the money problem football has created; Julie spends the same week trying to reach René, and drawing conclusions from how long that takes. Jonas Elmer keeps all of them inside a few rooms for ninety-two minutes and lets talk carry the weight, comedy and drama arriving in the same sentences instead of taking turns. It took the Bodil for best Danish film. A picture with this little plot lives on whether its performers can be left alone in a shot, and everything here — the fixed flat, the fixed week, the call that will not connect — is arranged to leave them alone as long as possible.

Caste is the one fact the household keeps from the girl it raised as a daughter. She came in as an orphan; the people who took her decided she did not need to know, and Bimal Roy gives that decision a hundred and sixty-one minutes — time enough to watch what a secret does to its keepers as well as to the person it is kept from. Years pass. She falls in love with a man of the family's own caste, and a private accommodation stops being private. Roy stays at domestic scale throughout: rooms, meals, the distance between how a daughter is treated and how she is introduced to visitors. Nothing is raised to a shout. The cruelty is in the courtesies, performed by people who think of themselves as kind and are never obliged to think again.
